beats.headline: Stop polling your database for changes.
beats.subline: Timestamp columns are a trap that will eventually drop your data.
beats.narration: Polling a timestamp column works until it doesn't. Hard deletes vanish before your next scan, and rapid updates collapse into the final state. You need Change Data Capture.

beats.title: Polling vs. Log Mining
beats.narration: Polling creates ghost records and competes with customer queries. CDC reads the database's own transaction log, capturing every single state transition in commit order.

beats.title: The CDC Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Mining the Transaction Log
beats.narration: Debezium attaches as a replication client. It reads the WAL or Binlog directly, turning binary mutations into structured Kafka events without touching your tables.

beats.title: The Change Envelope

steps.explanation: c=create, u=update, d=delete. Essential for downstream logic.
Before and after images of the row. Note: Postgres needs REPLICA IDENTITY FULL for full before-images.

beats.narration: The envelope gives you the full context. The op field defines the action, while before and after snapshots show the state change. It's the gold standard for audit trails.

beats.title: CDC Fundamentals Locked
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Kafka Connect architecture and the SMT magic →
beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we look at Kafka Connect internals and how to flatten these envelopes for your microservices.

beats.headline: Don't write custom producers.
beats.subline: Kafka Connect handles the heavy lifting of streaming data at scale.
beats.narration: Why write boilerplate code to move data? Kafka Connect is a distributed runtime that handles offsets, failures, and schema evolution out of the box.

beats.title: Connect Architecture
beats.subtitle: Worker JVMs and Internal Topics
beats.narration: Connect uses worker JVMs. Source tasks pull from the DB, SMTs reshape the data in-flight, and converters serialize it into Kafka. It's a plug-and-play pipeline.

beats.title: Flattening with SMTs

steps.explanation: Promotes the 'after' struct to the top level, removing the envelope complexity.
Injects op and timestamp into the flat payload for downstream audit.

beats.narration: Raw envelopes are noisy. The ExtractNewRecordState transform flattens the message, making it look like a standard domain event for your consumers.

beats.title: Connector Status
beats.caption: Monitoring your pipeline
beats.narration: Always monitor your connector status. Kafka Connect tracks its position in internal topics like connect-offsets. If it fails, that's where you find the resume point.

beats.title: Connectors Mastered
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: The Outbox Pattern for domain events →
beats.narration: Connect is powerful. In Part 3, we solve the dual-write problem using the Transactional Outbox pattern.

beats.headline: Stop dual-writing to DB and Kafka.
beats.subline: It's a recipe for distributed data inconsistency.
beats.narration: Writing to a DB and then sending to Kafka in two steps is a race condition waiting to happen. Use the Outbox pattern to make it atomic.

beats.title: Atomic Outbox
beats.subtitle: Single Transaction Writes
beats.narration: Update your business table and insert an event into an outbox table in one ACID transaction. Debezium reads that outbox row and streams it to Kafka.

beats.title: EventRouter SMT

steps.explanation: Turns raw outbox rows into clean domain events.
Routes events to topics based on the aggregate type field.

beats.narration: The EventRouter SMT is the secret sauce. It takes your outbox table rows and routes them to specific Kafka topics based on the aggregate type.

beats.title: Dual-Write vs. Outbox
beats.narration: Dual-writing is fragile. The Outbox pattern ensures your database and Kafka are always in sync because the event is part of the database transaction.

beats.title: Outbox Pattern Locked
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Schema evolution and DDL traps →
beats.narration: Outbox is the professional way to handle events. In Part 4, we look at how to handle schema changes without breaking your pipeline.

beats.headline: One ALTER TABLE can kill your pipeline.
beats.subline: MySQL and Postgres handle schema changes in fundamentally different ways.
beats.narration: Schema changes are inevitable. But if your connector doesn't understand the new column layout, your Kafka consumers will crash. Here is how to survive.

beats.title: MySQL vs Postgres DDL
beats.subtitle: History Topics vs. Metadata
beats.narration: MySQL writes DDL to a history topic. Postgres sends metadata messages before row events. Both require careful planning to avoid breaking downstream consumers.

beats.title: Schema History Topic
beats.caption: The MySQL safety net

lines.text: # NEVER compact the schema history topic!

beats.narration: For MySQL, your schema history topic is critical. It must have infinite retention and no compaction. If you lose this data, you cannot reconstruct your schema history.

beats.title: Schema Evolution Strategy

top.label: Breaking Changes
top.code: ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN total;

bottom.label: Safe Evolution
bottom.code: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status_code INT DEFAULT 0;

beats.narration: Treat DDL like a public API. Add nullable columns, backfill, then migrate. Dropping columns without coordination is a guaranteed production outage.

beats.title: Schema Strategy Locked

beats.headline: Your CDC connector can crash your database.
beats.subline: The Postgres WAL trap is the #1 cause of production outages.
beats.narration: If your connector falls behind, Postgres keeps the WAL logs forever. Eventually, the disk fills up, and your database halts. Here is the fix.

beats.title: The WAL Trap
beats.subtitle: Stalled Replication Slots
beats.narration: If Debezium stops, the replication slot stops advancing. Postgres refuses to recycle WAL logs. The disk fills, and your production database goes down.

beats.title: Heartbeat Configuration
beats.code:
"heartbeat.interval.ms": "30000",
"heartbeat.action.query": "UPDATE public.debezium_heartbeat SET updated_at = NOW() WHERE id = 1"

steps.explanation: Forces a heartbeat every 30 seconds to keep the slot alive.
Updates a dummy table to ensure log progression.

beats.narration: The heartbeat query forces the replication slot to advance even if your main tables are idle. It's the only way to ensure WAL logs get recycled safely.

beats.title: Monitoring Lag
beats.caption: Check your slot status

lines.text: SELECT slot_name, wal_status, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(...)) FROM pg_replication_slots;

beats.narration: Monitor your replication slots daily. If retained_wal starts growing, you have a problem. Set max_slot_wal_keep_size as a hard safety cap.
